summary: Describes the BEEP core, a generic application protocol kernel for connection-oriented, asynchronous interactions. It provides framing and multiplexing so new application protocols can be built on top. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Many apps need the same plumbing for sending messages back and forth. BEEP is a ready-made set of pipes that new programs can reuse.

subtitle: A reusable application protocol kernel: framing, channels and negotiation so new protocols need not rebuild them.

tldr.problem: Every new connection-oriented application protocol has to solve the same plumbing problems again: how to frame messages, how to run several exchanges at once, and how to add security and authentication.
tldr.mechanism: BEEP frames MIME messages and multiplexes independent numbered channels over one session. Channel zero manages the others, and each channel runs a profile; the RFC defines profiles for TLS and for SASL authentication.
tldr.outcome: Application designers define only their own data-exchange profiles and reuse the rest. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and leaves the binding to a transport, such as TCP, to a separate document.

today: RFC 3080 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It leaves the transport binding to separate mapping documents, such as RFC 3081 for TCP.

sections.title: What BEEP Is
sections.content:
RFC 3080 describes BEEP (Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol), a generic application protocol kernel for connection-oriented, asynchronous interactions. At its core is a framing mechanism that lets peers have simultaneous, independent exchanges of messages.

Messages are arbitrary MIME content, though they are usually textual and structured with XML. Every exchange happens on a channel, a binding to a well-defined aspect of the application such as transport security, user authentication or data exchange. Each channel has a profile that defines the syntax and meaning of its messages.

Besides channel management, the RFC defines the TLS transport security profile and a family of SASL profiles. Data-exchange profiles are left to application protocol designers.
sections.eli5: BEEP is a ready-made set of pipes for apps that need to send messages. Each pipe has its own job, and app builders only add the parts that are special to them.

sections.title: Sessions, Roles and Exchange Styles
sections.content:
A BEEP session maps onto an underlying transport service. A separate document describes each mapping; RFC 3080 cites one that maps a session onto a single TCP connection. When a session starts, each peer advertises its profiles, and later the client proposes one or more profiles for a new channel. The server picks one or declines.

Channels fall into two kinds. Initial tuning channels set things up, such as transport security, and go quiet early; only one tuning channel may exist at a time. Continuous channels carry data, and many may be in use at once.

Peers have two pairs of labels. The peer that waits for connections is in the listening role and the one that connects is initiating. Separately, the peer that starts an exchange is the client and the other is the server.

There are three exchange styles. In MSG/RPY the server performs the task and sends a positive reply. In MSG/ERR it declines with a negative reply. In MSG/ANS it sends zero or more ANS messages and ends with a NUL message. The first two are one-to-one exchanges and the last is one-to-many.
sections.eli5: One connection holds many channels, like lanes in a swimming pool. A request can get a single answer, an error, or a string of answers followed by a stop signal.

sections.title: Messages and Frames
sections.content:
A message follows MIME rules. If no headers are given, the default Content-Type is application/octet-stream and the default Content-Transfer-Encoding is binary. A message normally travels in one frame but may be split into several.

A frame is a header, a payload and the trailer END. The header and trailer are printable ASCII ending in a CRLF pair. The header has a keyword (MSG, RPY, ERR, ANS or NUL) followed by the channel number, message number, a continuation indicator, a sequence number and a payload size. ANS frames add an answer number.

The continuation indicator is a period (.) for the last frame of a message and an asterisk when more frames follow. The sequence number counts payload octets on each channel, modulo 232, so a receiver can tell what the next frame's number should be. Frames of a segmented message must be sent without other messages on the same channel in between, but frames on other channels, and ANS frames in one-to-many replies, may interleave.

A poorly-formed frame, a sequence number that is not the expected value, or a missing trailer means the session is terminated without a response, and logging a diagnostic is recommended.
sections.eli5: Each message goes in an envelope with a label saying which channel it belongs to, how big it is, and whether more envelopes are coming. If a label does not make sense, the whole conversation is hung up.

sections.title: Channel Management on Channel Zero
sections.content:
When a session starts only channel zero exists, and it handles channel management. A peer should support at least 257 concurrent channels. Each peer immediately sends a positive reply with message number zero containing a greeting element that lists its profiles. If a listener is unavailable it sends an error element instead, and both peers end the session.

To open a channel, a peer sends a start element with a channel number and one or more profile elements. Initiating peers use only odd channel numbers and listening peers only even ones, to avoid clashes. A profile may carry an initialization message of at most 4K octets. The reply is the chosen profile or an error.

To close a channel, a peer sends close with the channel number and a reply code, once all its MSG messages on that channel have been answered. The receiver can refuse with error, or accept with ok after it has finished its queued and outstanding exchanges. A close with number zero asks to release the whole session; if that is declined the session should not be terminated, if possible.

Errors carry a three-digit reply code, for example 200 for success, 421 for service not available and 550 when no requested profile is acceptable.
sections.eli5: Channel zero is the front desk. You ask it to open a new numbered room for a certain job, or to close one when you are done, and it can say no.

sections.title: Asynchrony and Peer-to-Peer Behavior
sections.content:
BEEP allows pipelining within a channel and parallelism between channels. A client may send several MSG messages on one channel without waiting for replies, but the server must process them in order and reply in the same order. On different channels, the server may process messages in any order, so there is no ordering of replies across channels.

A server may send a negative reply before it has received the final frame of a message, and must then ignore the rest of that message. A client that receives such a reply before it finishes sending must send a final MSG frame with a complete indicator and an empty payload.

BEEP is peer-to-peer, so both peers must be ready to receive every message defined in the memo, and all profiles must give a proper error reply to unexpected MSG messages. Message numbers only matter in one direction: numbers sent by the initiator are unrelated to those sent by the listener.
sections.eli5: You can hand in several requests at once, and different channels can work at the same time. On one channel, answers come back in the order you asked.

sections.title: Transport Security with TLS
sections.content:
A new BEEP session gives plaintext transfer, with no privacy. Security is added through an initial tuning profile. The RFC defines the TLS transport security profile, identified as http://iana.org/beep/TLS, based on TLS version one.

The client starts a channel with this profile and puts a ready element in the start message, optionally with a version attribute naming the earliest acceptable TLS version. The server answers with proceed or an error. After ready, a peer must send no more traffic on the transport until it gets a reply.

When negotiation begins, all channels including channel zero are implicitly closed. Whatever the outcome, both peers then send a new greeting, which may differ depending on whether privacy is now in use. Note that channel creation can succeed while the encapsulated operation fails, so a positive reply can carry an error inside it.
sections.eli5: Starting TLS is like asking to move the whole conversation into a soundproof room. Everyone leaves the old room, then introduces themselves again once inside.

sections.title: User Authentication with SASL
sections.content:
A new session gives anonymous access without trace information. User authentication is added by a family of profiles, one for each mechanism in the IANA SASL registry, identified as http://iana.org/beep/SASL/ followed by the mechanism name. The SASL service name is beep.

Challenges and responses travel in blob elements, always base64-encoded. The optional status attribute is abort (client gives up), complete (server reports success) or continue. A server signals failure with an error. After one successful authentication, the identity applies to all existing and future channels and no further attempts are allowed.

Once transport security is negotiated, a SASL security layer must not be negotiated, and the reverse. The SASL EXTERNAL mechanism relies on an outside authentication service, such as an active TLS profile. Authorization remains an internal matter for each peer, which may reject operations with error code 530.
sections.eli5: Showing your ID at the door once, after which everyone inside knows who you are for the rest of your visit.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The framing mechanism by itself gives no protection against attack. Protection comes from the tuning profiles. For SASL, the RFC points to the security considerations of the SASL specification.

With TLS or a SASL security layer, a man-in-the-middle may remove the security profiles from the greeting, or reject the ready element, so a peer may need to be configurable to refuse to proceed without enough privacy. An attacker may also push a down-negotiation to the weakest cipher suite, so peers should be configurable to refuse weak suites. Anything exchanged before a successful negotiation may be modified, so after negotiating, a peer must discard cached information about the session.

Because BEEP is peer-to-peer, each channel should apply access control based on the authenticated identity and privacy level before performing a task.
sections.eli5: The plain pipes are not private by themselves. Add the locks first, and check that a sneaky stranger did not talk you out of using them.

data.title: Start a channel
data.code:
MSG 0 1 . 52 120
Content-Type: application/beep+xml

<start number='1'>
   <profile uri='http://iana.org/beep/SASL/OTP' />
</start>
END

messages.note: Sent as soon as the session opens.

messages.label: start channel 1 with ready
messages.note: Asks to use the TLS profile.
